items.scenario: The agent is moving the payment service to a new database cluster (internal codename 'Kestrel', ticket PAY-2214, branch feat/kestrel-cutover). The director expects the release on Oct 9. Facts: (1) MEASURED: a load test on Oct 2 at twice normal traffic gave p99 checkout latency of 1.8 seconds, against a target of 300 ms. (2) MEASURED: the cause is the connection pooler in front of the new cluster. Its transaction mode does not work with the prepared statements the application uses, so every request opens a new connection. (3) ESTIMATE: the fix will take 3 to 5 engineer-days. (4) ESTIMATE: the earliest new release date is Oct 14, and that depends on the fix landing first time. (5) UNKNOWN: nobody has measured whether the fix brings latency all the way back to target. It may only get part of the way. (6) MEASURED: two enterprise customers, Acme Logistics and Northwind, were promised the feature by Oct 10. (7) MEASURED: current production still runs on the old cluster, is not affected, and no data has been lost. The agent's working notes contain a table of four load-test runs with columns headed only 'A/B/C/D'.

**What happened (measured).** A load test on Oct 2, at twice normal traffic, gave checkout latency of 1.8 seconds for the slowest 1% of requests (p99). The target is 300 ms.

**Cause (measured).** The connection pooler in front of the new cluster runs in a mode that does not work with the prepared statements our application uses. So every request opens a new database connection.

**Fix (estimate).** 3 to 5 engineer-days.

### What went wrong
- **Measured:** In a load test on Oct 2 at twice normal traffic, the slowest 1% of checkouts took 1.8 seconds. The target is 0.3 seconds.
- **Measured:** The cause is the component that manages database connections in front of the new database. It is set up in a way that does not work with how our application sends queries, so every request opens a brand-new database connection.

### What it means for the date
- **Estimate:** The fix takes 3 to 5 engineer-days.
- **Estimate:** Earliest release is Oct 14, and only if the fix works first time.
- **Unknown:** Nobody has yet measured whether the fix brings checkout all the way back to 0.3 seconds or only part of the way. Until the load test is re-run after the fix, treat Oct 14 as a best case, not a plan.

### Customer impact
Acme Logistics and Northwind were promised this feature by Oct 10. Even the best case misses that by four days. I suggest they hear this from us now rather than close to the date.

items.scenario: Customers say their order still shows 'awaiting payment' for a while after they have paid. The director will be asked about this at a board meeting next week and wants to understand the cause well enough to explain it. They do not need to fix it. The underlying concept is replication lag, also called eventual consistency. Engineers call the order-status page the 'CQRS read model' in the service known internally as 'Ledgerline'. Facts: (1) MEASURED: the order-status page reads from a database replica, not from the primary database where payments are written. (2) MEASURED last week: the replica is usually 2 to 5 seconds behind the primary, and up to 40 seconds behind at peak traffic. (3) MEASURED: 37 support tickets in September mentioned 'payment not showing'. (4) MEASURED: no payment has been lost or charged twice. The money is recorded correctly, and the page only shows it late. (5) ESTIMATE: there are known ways to remove the delay for the paying customer, at roughly 1 to 2 weeks of work. A decision on that may come later and is not being asked for now.
items.with:
**Payments are recorded correctly and at once. The order page shows them late because it reads from a copy of the database that runs a few seconds behind.**

*Step 1 of 3: the cause. Step 2: how long the delay is and how many customers notice it. Step 3: a short version you can say at the board.*

Payments are written to the main database. The order-status page does not read from that database. It reads from a copy, called a replica, which receives every change from the main database. Those changes take a little time to arrive. Until they do, the page still says 'awaiting payment', even though the payment is already recorded.

Engineers call this **replication lag**, or **eventual consistency**: the copy always catches up, but not instantly.

**No payment has been lost or charged twice (measured).** The money is right; only the page is late.

Does that explanation land?

- **Continue** - step 2: how long the delay is, and the support tickets it caused in September.
- **Explore** - more on eventual consistency as a general idea.
items.without:
**Short version:** Payments are recorded instantly and correctly. The order page reads from a copy of the database that runs a few seconds behind, so for a short time it can still show 'awaiting payment' after the customer has paid.

### How it works
We keep order data in two places:
- **The main database**, where a payment is written the moment it happens.
- **A copy (a 'replica')**, which is updated continuously from the main database. The order-status page reads from this copy.

This is a common design: page views go to the copy, so the main database is kept free for recording payments. The cost is that the copy is always slightly behind the main database. Engineers call this delay **replication lag**, and the general idea that the copy always catches up, just not instantly, is called **eventual consistency**.

An analogy: an airport departures board. A gate change goes into the airline's system first, and the board shows it a little later. The change is real the moment it is made; the board is just catching up.

### The numbers
- **Usual delay:** 2 to 5 seconds. **At peak traffic:** up to 40 seconds. (Measured last week.)
- **37 support tickets** in September mentioned 'payment not showing'.
- **No payment has been lost or charged twice.** Only the display is late.

### If the board asks whether it can be fixed
Yes. There are known ways to show the paying customer their up-to-date status straight away, at roughly 1 to 2 weeks of work (estimate). No decision is needed on that now.

### One sentence for the board
> The payment is recorded correctly the instant it is made. The status page reads from a copy that can lag by seconds, and up to 40 seconds at peak, so it sometimes shows the payment late. No money has been lost or double-charged.

items.scenario: Raw user-event data (clicks and page views) in the analytics warehouse is currently deleted after 30 days. The product team wants year-over-year comparisons for planning in January. Two decisions are needed, and the second depends on the first. Decision 1, how long to keep raw events: 90 days or 13 months. Decision 2, where to keep them: stay in the current warehouse, or move events older than 90 days to cheaper object storage. Facts: (1) MEASURED: legal counsel says 13 months requires a privacy-policy update and 30 days' notice to EU users. 90 days does not. (2) ESTIMATE: at 90 days the warehouse costs about $2,100 a month and no move is needed, so Decision 2 falls away. (3) ESTIMATE: at 13 months, keeping everything in the warehouse costs about $9,500 a month. A split, with 90 days in the warehouse and the rest in object storage, costs about $3,900 a month. Queries on the older data would take minutes, not seconds. (4) UNKNOWN: how often anyone queries data older than 90 days. This has not been measured. (5) DEADLINE: data older than 30 days is deleted on a rolling basis, and once deleted it cannot be recovered. The agent can pause the deletion job until Oct 15 without approval, but not after that. (6) RECOMMENDATION: 13 months with the split storage, with the EU notice sent this week. The agent also recommends pausing deletion now, so that waiting for the 30-day notice does not lose data.
